prompts.title: Digital footprint audit (self or client)
prompts.use: Map what is publicly visible about a person who asked you to do it.
prompts.prompt:
Act as an ethical OSINT analyst. I have written permission from [SUBJECT NAME] to assess their public digital footprint.
Known starting points: [USERNAMES / EMAIL / CITY / EMPLOYER].
1. List public source types I should check (search engines, social profiles, breach notification sites, data brokers, code repos).
2. For each, say what kind of exposure to look for and the privacy risk it creates.
3. Give a checklist I can work through manually and a remediation step for each finding.
Do not suggest accessing private accounts, guessing passwords or contacting the subject's contacts.
prompts.tip: Keep the written authorisation and scope with your notes. OSINT on someone who has not agreed can become stalking.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Company attack surface from public sources
prompts.use: Pre-engagement view of what an authorised client exposes online.
prompts.prompt:
I am doing an authorised external assessment for [ORGANISATION], engagement ID [ID], scope: [DOMAINS].
Using only passive, public sources, help me plan:
- Subdomain and certificate transparency review
- Public code and paste exposure (leaked keys, configs)
- Employee role exposure useful for phishing awareness training
- Third-party and SaaS footprint
Output a table: Source | What to look for | Why it matters | How to report it safely.
prompts.tip: Passive first. Do not touch anything outside the signed scope, even if it looks related.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Image verification checklist
prompts.use: Check whether a viral photo is real before you share or report it.
prompts.prompt:
Help me verify this image. Description: [WHAT THE IMAGE SHOWS]. Claimed place and date: [CLAIM].
Give me a step-by-step plan: reverse image search, metadata check, shadows and weather consistency, landmarks, earliest upload, signs of editing or AI generation.
End with a confidence rating template I can fill in, not a verdict.
prompts.tip: Treat AI 'this looks real' answers as hints. The evidence has to come from your own checks.
prompts.model: A model with strong step-by-step reasoning helps here. Check every claim it makes against the source.

prompts.title: Username pivot plan for a scam report
prompts.use: Organise public information about a scam account to hand to police or a platform.
prompts.prompt:
I am a victim of an online scam and want to prepare a report for the police and the platform.
Scammer handle(s): [HANDLES]. Platform: [PLATFORM]. Payment info shown to me: [UPI ID / ACCOUNT].
Help me list what public information to capture (profile URL, screenshots with timestamps, linked accounts) and how to store it as evidence.
Do not suggest contacting, threatening or hacking the scammer.
prompts.tip: Screenshot with the URL and clock visible, and keep the originals. Report on cybercrime.gov.in or call 1930 first if money moved.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: OSINT findings report
prompts.use: Turn raw notes into a clean, client-ready report.
prompts.prompt:
Convert these authorised OSINT notes into a report for [CLIENT].
Notes: [PASTE NOTES]
Structure: Scope and authorisation, Method (sources only), Findings ranked by risk, Evidence references, Recommendations, Limitations.
Remove any personal data that is not needed to explain a finding.
prompts.tip: Minimise personal data in the final report. Clients rarely need every detail you found.
prompts.model: Any strong writing model. Ask it to keep your tone and to flag claims it cannot support.

prompts.title: Scan plan for my own lab or approved scope
prompts.use: Choose safe nmap options before you run anything.
prompts.prompt:
I own or am authorised to scan: [TARGET RANGE / LAB]. Rules of engagement: [TIME WINDOW, RATE LIMITS, EXCLUSIONS].
Suggest an nmap plan in phases (host discovery, top ports, full TCP, service versions, safe scripts).
For each phase, give the command, what it does, noise level and when to stop.
Keep it low impact and within scope.
prompts.tip: Put the scope and contact person in the first line of your notes. If a host is not on the list, skip it.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Explain my nmap output
prompts.use: Understand open ports and services from a scan you ran.
prompts.prompt:
Explain this nmap output from my authorised scan of [ASSET]:
```
[PASTE OUTPUT]
```
For each open port: service, version, common misconfigurations to check, and a defensive fix. Then rank the top 3 risks and say what evidence would confirm each.
prompts.tip: Version banners can lie. Confirm before you write 'vulnerable' in a report.
prompts.model: A model with strong step-by-step reasoning helps here. Check every claim it makes against the source.

prompts.title: Triage nuclei results
prompts.use: Separate real findings from false positives.
prompts.prompt:
These are nuclei results from an authorised scan of [SCOPE]:
```
[PASTE RESULTS]
```
Group by severity. For each, say whether it is likely a true positive, how to verify it manually without causing harm, and the fix. Flag anything that needs the asset owner's attention today.
prompts.tip: Templates are only as good as their matchers. Re-test critical items by hand.
prompts.model: Use a model with a long context window so the full log or report fits in one go. Never paste secrets or client data into a tool your organisation has not approved.

prompts.title: Read a nikto report
prompts.use: Turn web server scan noise into an action list.
prompts.prompt:
Here is a nikto report for my own web server [HOST]:
```
[PASTE REPORT]
```
List findings that matter, explain each in plain English, and give the exact config change (Apache/Nginx/IIS: [SERVER]) to fix it. Mark informational items separately.
prompts.tip: Nikto is loud. Only run it where noise is acceptable and approved.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Hardening checklist after a scan
prompts.use: Close what the scan found on assets you manage.
prompts.prompt: Based on these findings for my systems [SUMMARY OF FINDINGS], write a hardening checklist grouped by: network exposure, service configuration, patching, authentication, logging. Include how to re-scan to confirm each fix.
prompts.tip: Re-scan after fixing and keep the before and after as proof for the asset owner.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Alert triage in five questions
prompts.use: Decide quickly if an alert is real.
prompts.prompt:
Act as a tier 2 SOC analyst. Alert: [ALERT NAME]. Raw event:
```
[PASTE EVENT]
```
Answer: What happened? Is it expected for this asset [ASSET ROLE]? What else should I query to confirm? True positive, benign, or needs more data? What is the next action and who owns it?
prompts.tip: Write down why you closed an alert. Future you will thank you during the audit.
prompts.model: A model with strong step-by-step reasoning helps here. Check every claim it makes against the source.

prompts.title: Windows event log story
prompts.use: Rebuild a timeline from Windows events.
prompts.prompt:
Here are Windows events (4624, 4625, 4688, 4672, 7045 and others) from host [HOST]:
```
[PASTE EVENTS]
```
Build a timeline in a table: time, event ID, account, process, what it means. Then highlight suspicious sequences and the MITRE ATT&CK technique they may map to.
prompts.tip: Normalise all times to one zone (say IST or UTC) before you compare sources.
prompts.model: Use a model with a long context window so the full log or report fits in one go. Never paste secrets or client data into a tool your organisation has not approved.

prompts.title: Write a detection query
prompts.use: Turn an idea into a SIEM query.
prompts.prompt:
Write a [SPLUNK SPL / KQL / ELASTIC EQL] query to detect [BEHAVIOUR, e.g. many failed logins then a success from a new country].
Data source fields: [FIELD NAMES].
Explain each line, likely false positives, and a tuning suggestion.
prompts.tip: Test on a week of real data before you turn it into an alert.
prompts.model: A code-focused model or a general model with strong coding skills. Keep code you are not allowed to share out of public tools.

prompts.title: Linux auth log review
prompts.use: Spot brute force and odd sudo use.
prompts.prompt:
Review this /var/log/auth.log excerpt from my server [HOST]:
```
[PASTE LOG]
```
Summarise failed and successful SSH logins by IP and user, any sudo use, new users or keys, and anything worth escalating. Suggest fail2ban or sshd_config changes.
prompts.tip: Remove real usernames and public IPs if you use a tool outside your organisation.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Shift handover note
prompts.use: Hand over cleanly to the next shift.
prompts.prompt:
Write a SOC shift handover from these notes: [NOTES].
Sections: Open incidents (status, owner, next step), Alerts under watch, Changes made, Blockers, Things the next shift must do in the first hour.
prompts.tip: Keep it short. If the next shift has to ask you a question, the note was missing something.
prompts.model: Any strong writing model. Ask it to keep your tone and to flag claims it cannot support.

prompts.title: First hour plan
prompts.use: Start an incident without missing the basics.
prompts.prompt:
We suspect [INCIDENT TYPE, e.g. ransomware, account takeover] at [ORGANISATION]. What we know: [FACTS].
Give a first-hour checklist: who to call, what to preserve, containment options with trade-offs, what not to do (e.g. wiping machines), and what to log. Include India-specific duties such as reporting listed incidents to CERT-In within 6 hours of noticing the incident or being told of it.
prompts.tip: Preserve evidence before you clean. Rebuilding a machine too early erases the story.
prompts.model: A model with strong step-by-step reasoning helps here. Check every claim it makes against the source.

prompts.title: Containment decision
prompts.use: Weigh isolating a system against keeping the business running.
prompts.prompt:
Asset: [ASSET], business role: [ROLE]. Threat signs: [SIGNS].
Compare options: network isolate, disable account, block IOC at firewall, keep monitoring. For each give risk, business impact, evidence impact and who must approve.
prompts.tip: Get the decision and the approver in writing in the incident log.
prompts.model: A model with strong step-by-step reasoning helps here. Check every claim it makes against the source.

prompts.title: Evidence collection list
prompts.use: Collect the right artefacts in the right order.
prompts.prompt: For a [WINDOWS / LINUX / M365 / AWS] incident on [ASSET], list artefacts to collect in order of volatility, the tool or console to use, and how to record hash and chain of custody. Keep it to what a defender on our side can legally collect.
prompts.tip: Hash every file you collect and note who handled it and when. In India this supports a BSA Section 63 certificate later.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Stakeholder update
prompts.use: Explain an incident to leadership without jargon.
prompts.prompt:
Write a short incident update for [AUDIENCE: CEO / board / customers]. Facts: [FACTS]. Unknowns: [UNKNOWNS].
Include: what happened, impact so far, what we are doing, what we need from them, next update time. Do not speculate beyond the facts.
prompts.tip: Say what you do not know yet. Overconfident early updates cause trouble later.
prompts.model: Any strong writing model. Ask it to keep your tone and to flag claims it cannot support.

prompts.title: Post-incident review
prompts.use: Learn from it without blame.
prompts.prompt:
Run a blameless post-incident review from this timeline: [TIMELINE].
Output: summary, root cause and contributing factors, what went well, what to improve, actions with owner and due date.
prompts.tip: Actions without an owner and a date do not happen.
prompts.model: Any strong writing model. Ask it to keep your tone and to flag claims it cannot support.

prompts.title: Summarise a threat report for my org
prompts.use: Find what matters to you in a long vendor report.
prompts.prompt:
Summarise this threat report for [ORGANISATION, SECTOR, TECH STACK]:
[PASTE REPORT OR KEY PARTS]
Output: 5-line summary, TTPs mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, IOCs as a table, whether it is relevant to us and why, 3 actions for this week.
prompts.tip: Indicators age fast. Behaviours (TTPs) last longer and make better detections.
prompts.model: Use a model with a long context window so the full log or report fits in one go. Never paste secrets or client data into a tool your organisation has not approved.

prompts.title: IOC enrichment plan
prompts.use: Decide what to check for each indicator.
prompts.prompt: For these indicators [IPs / DOMAINS / HASHES], list which public reputation and sandbox services to check, what each result means, and how to decide block, monitor or ignore. Output a table I can fill in.
prompts.tip: Never submit client files to public sandboxes without permission. Submit the hash first.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Threat profile of an actor
prompts.use: Brief your team on a group targeting your sector.
prompts.prompt:
Build a brief on [THREAT ACTOR] using only these sources: [SOURCES OR NOTES].
Sections: aliases, targeting, common initial access, tools, notable campaigns, detection ideas. Mark anything not in the sources as 'unconfirmed'.
prompts.tip: Ask the model to cite which source each line came from. Drop anything it cannot cite.
prompts.model: A model with strong step-by-step reasoning helps here. Check every claim it makes against the source.

prompts.title: Intelligence requirement writer
prompts.use: Ask the right questions before collecting intel.
prompts.prompt:
Help me write priority intelligence requirements for [ORGANISATION]. Business: [WHAT WE DO]. Crown jewels: [ASSETS]. Recent worries: [WORRIES].
Give 5 requirements, why each matters, and sources to answer them.
prompts.tip: If an intel item does not answer a requirement, you probably do not need it.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Weekly threat digest
prompts.use: A short Monday brief for your team.
prompts.prompt:
Turn these items into a one-page weekly threat digest for [TEAM]: [ITEMS].
For each: headline, why it matters to us, action (patch, hunt, watch, none). Keep it under 300 words.
prompts.tip: Same format every week makes it easy to skim.
prompts.model: Any strong writing model. Ask it to keep your tone and to flag claims it cannot support.

prompts.title: Explain a sandbox report
prompts.use: Understand what a sample did in a sandbox you ran.
prompts.prompt:
Explain this sandbox report for a sample from our environment:
```
[PASTE REPORT]
```
Summarise behaviour (processes, files, registry, network), likely family if the report says so, MITRE techniques, IOCs, and detections I can add. Separate facts from guesses.
prompts.tip: Run samples only in an isolated lab or an approved sandbox, never on your own laptop.
prompts.model: Use a model with a long context window so the full log or report fits in one go. Never paste secrets or client data into a tool your organisation has not approved.

prompts.title: Static triage from strings and PE info
prompts.use: First look at a suspicious file without running it.
prompts.prompt:
Here are strings, imports and PE header details from a suspicious file (hash [SHA256]):
```
[PASTE OUTPUT]
```
What capabilities do these suggest? Which indicators are strongest? What should I check next in a safe lab?
prompts.tip: Packed files hide their strings. Low string count plus high entropy often means packing.
prompts.model: A model with strong step-by-step reasoning helps here. Check every claim it makes against the source.

prompts.title: YARA rule review
prompts.use: Improve a detection rule for your own hunting.
prompts.prompt:
Review this YARA rule for false positives and robustness:
```
[PASTE RULE]
```
Suggest improvements, explain each condition, and give test ideas using known-good files from our environment.
prompts.tip: Test rules against a big set of clean files before you deploy them.
prompts.model: A code-focused model or a general model with strong coding skills. Keep code you are not allowed to share out of public tools.

prompts.title: Malware analysis report
prompts.use: Write findings for the SOC and management.
prompts.prompt:
Write a malware analysis report from these notes: [NOTES].
Sections: executive summary, sample details (hashes, names), behaviour, IOCs table, detections, remediation, open questions.
prompts.tip: Put defanged IOCs (example[.]com) in reports so nobody clicks them by accident.
prompts.model: Any strong writing model. Ask it to keep your tone and to flag claims it cannot support.

prompts.title: Suspicious macro document
prompts.use: Decide if an Office file is dangerous.
prompts.prompt:
Here is olevba or similar output for a document from a user's inbox:
```
[PASTE OUTPUT]
```
Explain what the macro tries to do, risk level, IOCs, and what to tell the user. Do not rewrite or improve the macro.
prompts.tip: Ask users how they got the file. The delivery path is half the story.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Email header analysis
prompts.use: Find where an email really came from.
prompts.prompt:
Analyse these email headers:
```
[PASTE HEADERS]
```
Show the hop path, sending IP and domain, SPF, DKIM and DMARC results, any mismatch between From, Return-Path and Reply-To, and a verdict with reasons.
prompts.tip: Read Received headers from bottom to top. The lowest one is closest to the sender.
prompts.model: A model with strong step-by-step reasoning helps here. Check every claim it makes against the source.

prompts.title: Is this email phishing?
prompts.use: Quick check for a staff member's report.
prompts.prompt:
A user reported this email (links defanged):
[PASTE BODY]
List red flags, what the attacker wants, whether to block sender or domain, and a friendly reply to the user thanking them.
prompts.tip: Thank every reporter. People report more when they are not made to feel silly.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Phishing awareness micro lesson
prompts.use: Train staff in five minutes.
prompts.prompt: Write a 5-minute phishing awareness lesson for [AUDIENCE, e.g. accounts team in India]. Include 3 realistic examples (UPI refund, KYC update, fake invoice), the clues in each, and what to do: report to IT, call 1930 if money moved.
prompts.tip: Use local examples. 'KYC expired' lands better in India than generic examples.
prompts.model: Any strong writing model. Ask it to keep your tone and to flag claims it cannot support.

prompts.title: DMARC rollout plan
prompts.use: Protect your domain from spoofing.
prompts.prompt:
Plan a DMARC rollout for [DOMAIN]. Current SPF: [SPF]. DKIM: [STATUS]. Senders: [LIST OF SERVICES].
Give steps from p=none to p=reject, how to read aggregate reports, and common breakages.
prompts.tip: Find every service that sends as your domain before you move to reject.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Phishing simulation plan (internal, approved)
prompts.use: Run an approved awareness test.
prompts.prompt:
Plan an internal phishing simulation approved by [APPROVER] for [ORGANISATION].
Cover: goals, audience, scenarios with difficulty levels, landing page that teaches, metrics, and how to communicate results without shaming people.
prompts.tip: Get HR and leadership approval in writing. Never collect real passwords in a simulation.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: IAM policy review
prompts.use: Find over-broad permissions.
prompts.prompt:
Review this [AWS / Azure / GCP] IAM policy for our account:
```
[PASTE POLICY]
```
Flag wildcards, privilege escalation paths, missing conditions, and give a least-privilege rewrite with explanations.
prompts.tip: Use access logs to see what a role actually uses, then trim the rest.
prompts.model: A code-focused model or a general model with strong coding skills. Keep code you are not allowed to share out of public tools.

prompts.title: Storage exposure check
prompts.use: Make sure buckets and blobs are not public by mistake.
prompts.prompt: Give me a checklist and CLI commands to review [S3 / Azure Blob / GCS] storage in my own account for public access, encryption, logging, versioning and lifecycle rules. Explain what a good result looks like.
prompts.tip: Turn on account-level public access blocks so a single mistake cannot expose data.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Read a CSPM findings export
prompts.use: Prioritise cloud posture findings.
prompts.prompt:
Here is an export from our cloud posture tool:
```
[PASTE FINDINGS]
```
Group duplicates, rank by real risk (internet exposure, data sensitivity, privilege), and give a 2-week fix plan.
prompts.tip: Severity labels from tools ignore your context. Re-rank by exposure and data.
prompts.model: Use a model with a long context window so the full log or report fits in one go. Never paste secrets or client data into a tool your organisation has not approved.

prompts.title: Terraform security review
prompts.use: Catch misconfigurations before deploy.
prompts.prompt:
Review this Terraform for security issues:
```
[PASTE CODE]
```
Check network exposure, encryption, logging, secrets in code, IAM. Give fixed code and explain each change.
prompts.tip: Add a policy scanner to CI so these checks run on every pull request.
prompts.model: A code-focused model or a general model with strong coding skills. Keep code you are not allowed to share out of public tools.

prompts.title: Cloud logging baseline
prompts.use: Make sure you can investigate later.
prompts.prompt: For our [CLOUD] setup with services [SERVICES], list the logs to enable, where to store them, retention (CERT-In expects 180 days for ICT logs in India), and 5 alerts to start with.
prompts.tip: Logs you did not turn on before an incident cannot be recovered after it.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Security review of a function
prompts.use: Find bugs in a piece of your code.
prompts.prompt:
Review this [LANGUAGE] code for security issues:
```
[PASTE CODE]
```
Check input validation, injection, auth, secrets, error handling. For each issue: line, risk, why, fixed code.
prompts.tip: Paste only code you are allowed to share. Strip keys and internal hostnames.
prompts.model: A code-focused model or a general model with strong coding skills. Keep code you are not allowed to share out of public tools.

prompts.title: Threat model a feature
prompts.use: Think like an attacker before you build.
prompts.prompt:
Threat model this feature using STRIDE: [FEATURE DESCRIPTION, DATA FLOWS, USERS].
Output a table: threat, STRIDE category, impact, likelihood, mitigation, test to prove it.
prompts.tip: Draw the data flow first. Most threats sit where data crosses a trust boundary.
prompts.model: A model with strong step-by-step reasoning helps here. Check every claim it makes against the source.

prompts.title: Explain a SAST finding
prompts.use: Decide if a scanner finding is real.
prompts.prompt:
Our scanner flagged this:
Rule: [RULE]
Code:
```
[PASTE CODE]
```
Is it a true positive? Explain the data flow from source to sink, and give a fix or a reason to suppress.
prompts.tip: Document every suppression with a reason so reviewers can trust the scan.
prompts.model: A code-focused model or a general model with strong coding skills. Keep code you are not allowed to share out of public tools.

prompts.title: Dependency risk review
prompts.use: Check third-party packages.
prompts.prompt:
Here is our dependency list and audit output:
```
[PASTE]
```
Rank vulnerable packages by exploitability in our use, suggest safe upgrade versions, and flag abandoned packages.
prompts.tip: A vulnerable function you never call is lower risk, but still plan the upgrade.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Secure coding checklist for a pull request
prompts.use: A reviewer's checklist for your stack.
prompts.prompt: Write a secure code review checklist for pull requests in [STACK, e.g. Node.js + PostgreSQL]. Keep it to 15 checks, each with a one-line example of bad and good code.
prompts.tip: Short checklists get used. Long ones get skipped.
prompts.model: A code-focused model or a general model with strong coding skills. Keep code you are not allowed to share out of public tools.

prompts.title: Write a policy draft
prompts.use: First draft of an internal policy.
prompts.prompt:
Draft a [POLICY NAME, e.g. Acceptable Use] policy for [ORGANISATION, SIZE, SECTOR] in India.
Sections: purpose, scope, roles, policy statements, exceptions, enforcement, review cycle. Plain English. Mark where legal review is needed (IT Act, DPDP Act, CERT-In Directions).
prompts.tip: A lawyer should review anything that creates obligations for staff or customers.
prompts.model: Any strong writing model. Ask it to keep your tone and to flag claims it cannot support.

prompts.title: Control mapping
prompts.use: Map one control set to another.
prompts.prompt: Map these controls [LIST] from [FRAMEWORK A, e.g. ISO 27001:2022 Annex A] to [FRAMEWORK B, e.g. NIST CSF 2.0]. Table: control, mapped control, fit (full, partial), gap notes. Say when you are unsure.
prompts.tip: Check every mapping against the official framework text. Models mix up control numbers.
prompts.model: A model with strong step-by-step reasoning helps here. Check every claim it makes against the source.

prompts.title: Risk register entry
prompts.use: Write a clear, scored risk.
prompts.prompt: Write risk register entries for these issues: [ISSUES]. For each: risk statement (cause, event, impact), likelihood, impact, current controls, treatment, owner, review date.
prompts.tip: A good risk statement names a cause, an event and an impact.
prompts.model: Any strong writing model. Ask it to keep your tone and to flag claims it cannot support.

prompts.title: DPDP readiness questions
prompts.use: Start a DPDP Act gap check.
prompts.prompt: Create a DPDP Act 2023 readiness questionnaire for [ORGANISATION] covering notice, consent, purpose limits, data principal rights, children's data, breach notification, retention and processors. Mark items that depend on DPDP Rules 2025 timelines.
prompts.tip: Most DPDP Rules obligations start 18 months after 13 Nov 2025. Plan now, verify dates with counsel.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Audit evidence request list
prompts.use: Prepare for an audit.
prompts.prompt: Create an evidence request list for an audit of [SCOPE] against [STANDARD]. For each control area list the evidence, who owns it and the format.

prompts.title: Scam News Story to Hinglish Reel Script
prompts.use: Turn a verified Indian scam news report into a 30 to 45 second awareness Reel in Hinglish.
prompts.prompt: You are a cyber awareness scriptwriter for an Indian Instagram and YouTube Shorts page called [PAGE NAME], aimed at [AUDIENCE, e.g. working adults in Mumbai and Palghar]. Case status: [UNDER INVESTIGATION / CHARGESHEETED / CONVICTED]. Write a [30/45/60] second Reel script in natural Hinglish (Roman script). prompts.tip: Paste the actual article text instead of a headline so the AI does not invent details, and always re-read the final script against the source before recording.

prompts.title: Marathi Cyber Awareness Reel

prompts.title: Instagram Carousel Outline

Use only the facts I provide below; if something is missing, write [NEEDS INFO] instead of guessing. Topic: [TOPIC]. Facts and examples: [FACTS]. Language: [HINGLISH / ENGLISH / MARATHI]. Brand style: [e.g. navy background, cyan and red accents]. Create a 7 slide carousel outline. Slide 1: cover with an alert tag and a question hook (max 7 words). prompts.tip: Write slide 1 last. Once the inner slides are clear, the strongest hook is usually the most surprising fact from slide 2 or 3 turned into a question.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: YouTube Long-Form Explainer Script

prompts.prompt: You are a YouTube scriptwriter for an Indian cyber awareness channel, [CHANNEL NAME], presented by [PRESENTER NAME] in [HINGLISH / HINDI / ENGLISH]. Use only the facts I provide below; if something is missing, write [NEEDS INFO] instead of guessing. Topic: [TOPIC]. Verified facts, stats and sources: [FACTS WITH SOURCES]. Target length: [MINUTES]. Viewer: [AUDIENCE]. Structure: 1) Cold open (first 30 seconds) with a relatable situation, no clickbait claims. 2) What the scam is. 3) Why people fall for it (psychology: urgency, authority, fear, greed). 4) Red flags checklist. 5) What to do in the first hour if it happens: call 1930, report on cybercrime.gov.in, contact the bank, preserve evidence. 6) Common myths. 7) Recap and CTA. prompts.tip: Ask the AI for the script first, then in a second message ask it to cut 15 percent. Tighter scripts hold retention much better.

prompts.title: Explain a Cyber Law Section in Simple Hinglish

If I have not pasted it, say you need the official text and do not reconstruct it from memory. Output: 1) One line meaning in Hinglish. 2) Explanation in 4 to 6 short bullets: what act is covered, who it applies to, what the penalty or consequence is as stated in the text. 3) Two everyday Indian examples that are clearly hypothetical. 4) Common misunderstandings. 5) 'Victim ho toh kya kare' with 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in if the section relates to a cybercrime. 6) Closing disclaimer: this is general information, consult a qualified lawyer for your case. Constraints: do not cite case law or amendments unless I provide them; flag any old IPC to BNS mapping as 'verify with official text'.
prompts.tip: Always paste the section from an official government source such as indiacode.nic.in. Models often mix up IPC and BNS numbering.

prompts.title: Real Case Study Explainer (Law Plus Lesson)
prompts.use: Explain a reported Indian cybercrime case by linking what happened to the relevant laws and the safety lesson.
prompts.prompt: You are a cyber law and awareness educator. Use only the facts I provide below; if something is missing, write [NEEDS INFO] instead of guessing. Case summary from a reputable news source: [PASTE SUMMARY]. Source and date: [SOURCE]. Current case status: [STATUS]. Sections reportedly invoked by police (as reported): [SECTIONS OR UNKNOWN]. Write an explainer for [FORMAT: Reel script / LinkedIn post / blog section] in [LANGUAGE]. Structure: what reportedly happened (neutral language), which legal provisions were reported and what they broadly cover, what the victim did right or could have done, 3 safety lessons, how to report (1930, cybercrime.gov.in). Rules: if the case is not concluded, do not name accused individuals or companies and use 'allegedly' or 'as per police'; never present allegations as proven; do not speculate about guilt; do not describe attack techniques in reproducible detail; do not identify the victim. End with: for any legal situation, consult a lawyer.
prompts.tip: Note the article date in your content. Case status changes fast, and an 'allegedly' that turns into an acquittal can create defamation risk if you named someone.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: DPDP Act 2023 Readiness Checklist for a Small Business

You give general guidance, not legal advice. Use only the facts I provide below; if something is missing, write [NEEDS INFO] instead of guessing. Business type: [TYPE]. Size: [EMPLOYEES]. Personal data collected: [e.g. names, phone numbers, Aadhaar copies, health records, student data]. How it is collected: [FORMS / WHATSAPP / WEBSITE / CCTV]. Where it is stored: [EXCEL / GOOGLE DRIVE / BILLING SOFTWARE / PAPER]. Who has access: [ROLES]. Third parties used: [e.g. payment gateway, SMS vendor]. Any children's data: [YES / NO]. Create a checklist grouped into: notice and consent, purpose limitation and data minimisation, security safeguards, data principal rights (access, correction, erasure, grievance), children's data, vendors and processors, retention and deletion, breach handling. For each item give: the action in plain English, priority (High / Medium / Low), effort (Quick win / Project), and an owner role. prompts.title: Data Breach Response Plan for an SME
prompts.use: Prepare a one-page incident response plan an Indian small business can follow when personal data is exposed.
prompts.prompt: You are an incident response consultant writing for a non-technical small business owner in India. Use only the facts I provide below; if something is missing, write [NEEDS INFO] instead of guessing. Business: [TYPE AND SIZE]. IT setup: [e.g. 5 laptops, Google Workspace, Tally, website on shared hosting]. IT support: [IN-HOUSE / VENDOR NAME / NONE]. Key data: [LIST]. Write a breach response plan with phases: 1) Detect and confirm, 2) Contain (first 60 minutes), 3) Preserve evidence, 4) Assess what data and whose data, 5) Notify (affected people, the Data Protection Board as required under DPDP once its breach rules are in force (about 13 May 2027), CERT-In where its directions apply, police or cybercrime.gov.in if a crime is involved, bank if money is involved), 6) Recover, 7) Review and improve. For each phase: what to do, who does it, and a one-line 'do not do this' warning (e.g. do not wipe the affected laptop before evidence is preserved). prompts.tip: Print the plan and keep a copy offline. During ransomware or an account takeover, the shared drive where the plan is stored may be the thing that is locked.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Cybercrime Complaint Draft for cybercrime.gov.in

Bank and branch: [BANK, BRANCH]. Account holder: [NAME]. Account or card (last 4 digits only): [XXXX]. Transaction details (date, time, amount, UTR or reference): [LIST]. How it happened: [SUMMARY]. Remedy sought: [e.g. reversal, block, investigation, written response]. Mention that I am aware of the RBI framework on customer liability for unauthorised electronic banking transactions and the Reserve Bank Integrated Ombudsman Scheme 2026 (RB-IOS 2026, cms.rbi.org.in) as an escalation path, but do not quote specific day limits or liability rules unless I paste the current RBI text. Keep under 350 words. Add a separate checklist of attachments. Note at the end: for disputed liability, consult a lawyer or consumer forum advisor.

prompts.title: Digital Evidence Preservation Checklist

For sextortion or image abuse, add the option of reporting directly to the platform and note that the victim is not at fault. prompts.use: Write an authentic LinkedIn post documenting a SOC learning milestone, lab, or lesson.
prompts.prompt: You are a LinkedIn ghostwriter for an early-career cybersecurity professional in India targeting Junior SOC Analyst roles. Use only the facts I provide below; if something is missing, write [NEEDS INFO] instead of guessing. My role and background: [e.g. IT Support Engineer, BCA, law student]. What I did or learned: [DETAILS: lab, room, tool, cert, ticket lesson]. Tools involved: [e.g. Splunk, Wazuh, Wireshark, Sysmon]. One concrete result or screenshot description: [RESULT]. Post goal: [VISIBILITY / RECRUITER INTEREST / COMMUNITY]. Write a post of 150 to 220 words: a first line hook under 12 words with no clickbait, the context in 2 lines, what I did in 3 short steps, the one lesson, a question to invite comments. Suggest one visual (diagram or redacted screenshot) and 3 to 5 hashtags. Rules: no exaggeration of skills or results, no claim of certs I have not earned, no client or employer confidential data, redact IPs, hostnames and usernames from real environments; only lab or permitted data. Avoid buzzword stacking. Give 2 versions: one more personal, one more technical.
prompts.tip: Put links in the first comment and reply to every comment in the first hour. Early engagement matters more than hashtags.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Junior SOC Analyst Interview Prep with Mock Q&A
prompts.use: Run a realistic mock interview for an L1 SOC Analyst role in India.
prompts.prompt: You are a senior SOC manager at an Indian MSSP or global capability centre interviewing candidates for a SOC Analyst L1 role. Use only the facts I provide below; if something is missing, write [NEEDS INFO] instead of guessing. Job description: [PASTE JD]. My background: [SUMMARY]. My projects and labs: [LIST]. Certs done or in progress: [LIST]. Interview round: [HR / TECHNICAL / SCENARIO]. Run the mock interview one question at a time and wait for my answer. Cover: networking basics (TCP/IP, DNS, ports), Windows and Linux logs, SIEM concepts, the alert triage process, phishing analysis, the incident response lifecycle, MITRE ATT&CK at a high level, a scenario question, and 'tell me about a project'. After each of my answers, give: a score out of 5, what was good, what was missing, and a model answer of max 120 words. At the end, give a summary of my 3 strongest and 3 weakest areas with a 7 day study plan. Keep the questions defensive and realistic for L1; do not ask me to perform attacks.
prompts.tip: Answer out loud and type afterwards. The real interview is spoken, and typing lets you over-polish answers you would not say that way.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Homelab Write-Up as an Incident Report
prompts.use: Turn a homelab exercise into a professional incident report for GitHub or a portfolio.
prompts.prompt: You are a SOC team lead who reviews incident reports. Help me turn my homelab work into a portfolio-quality incident report. Use only the facts I provide below; if something is missing, write [NEEDS INFO] instead of guessing. Lab setup: [e.g. Windows 10 VM with Sysmon, Wazuh manager, Kali attacker VM, all on an isolated host-only network that I own]. Simulated activity I ran in my own lab: [DESCRIPTION]. Alerts and logs observed: [PASTE KEY LOG LINES, REDACTED]. Actions I took: [LIST]. Write a report with: Title, Executive summary (3 lines), Environment and scope (state clearly that this was an authorised isolated lab), Timeline table, Detection (which rule or log fired and why), Analysis (mapping to MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs only if I supplied them or they clearly match; otherwise suggest and mark [VERIFY]), Containment and remediation steps, Lessons learned, Detection improvement ideas. Rules: focus on detection and response; do not include weaponised commands or payloads; describe attacker steps only at a high level. Output in Markdown suitable for a GitHub README, with placeholders for screenshots.
prompts.tip: Hiring managers read the executive summary and the detection section first. Make those two sections strong before polishing the rest.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Resume Bullet Polishing for SOC Roles
prompts.use: Rewrite IT support and project experience into honest, impact-focused resume bullets for SOC applications.
prompts.prompt: You are a cybersecurity recruiter in India who screens resumes for SOC L1 roles. Use only the facts I provide below; if something is missing, write [NEEDS INFO] instead of guessing. Target role and JD keywords: [PASTE]. My current bullets: [PASTE]. Real numbers I can stand behind: [e.g. tickets per week, users supported, labs completed]. Rewrite each bullet using the pattern action verb, what, tool, measurable result. Highlight security-relevant parts of IT support work (access management, endpoint hygiene, phishing reports handled, patching, backups). Rules: never invent numbers, tools or responsibilities; if a bullet has no metric, suggest what I could measure and mark it [ADD METRIC]; keep each bullet under 25 words; avoid buzzwords like 'rockstar' or 'ninja'. Output a table: Original, Rewritten, Keywords matched. Then list 5 JD keywords I am missing and an honest way to close each gap.
prompts.tip: Tailor the top three bullets for each application. Recruiters often scan only those before deciding.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: College Phishing-Awareness Session Script
prompts.use: Create a 45 minute interactive phishing awareness session for college students.
prompts.prompt: You are a cyber awareness trainer who runs sessions in Indian colleges. Use only the facts I provide below; if something is missing, write [NEEDS INFO] instead of guessing. College and audience: [COLLEGE, YEAR, STREAM, APPROX SIZE]. Language: [HINGLISH / ENGLISH / MARATHI]. Time: [MINUTES]. Recent local scam examples I want to use: [LIST WITH SOURCES]. Resources available: [PROJECTOR / NO PROJECTOR]. Create a session plan with: icebreaker poll, what phishing is (email, SMS smishing, voice vishing, WhatsApp, QR code), 5 real-style examples with red flags (use fictional names, numbers and domains like example.com, never live malicious links), a live 'spot the phish' activity, fake internship and job scam section relevant to students, what to do if you clicked, reporting (1930, cybercrime.gov.in, Chakshu on Sancharsaathi for suspicious calls and SMS), and a closing pledge or quiz. Rules: awareness only; do not teach how to build phishing pages or kits; no shaming of victims. Output: a minute-by-minute agenda table, speaker notes for each segment, and a one-page take-home handout.
prompts.tip: Get the college's permission before running any simulated phishing test. Never send fake phishing to students without written approval from the institution.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Cyber Safety Quiz Generator
prompts.use: Generate quiz questions for a workshop, Instagram story poll or Google Form.
prompts.prompt: You are an instructional designer creating cyber safety quizzes for Indian audiences. Use only the facts I provide below; if something is missing, write [NEEDS INFO] instead of guessing. Topic(s): [TOPICS]. Audience: [STUDENTS / EMPLOYEES / SENIORS / GENERAL]. Difficulty: [EASY / MEDIUM / HARD]. Number of questions: [N]. Format: [MCQ / TRUE-FALSE / SCENARIO]. Language: [LANGUAGE]. For each question give: the question, 4 options (for MCQ), the correct answer, and a one-line explanation that teaches the safe behaviour. Use realistic Indian scenarios (UPI collect requests, KYC update SMS, courier or customs calls, 'digital arrest' calls, fake job offers) with fictional names and numbers. Rules: protective knowledge only; explanations should mention 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in where reporting is relevant. Also output a version formatted for Instagram story polls (question under 80 characters, 2 options).
prompts.tip: Make wrong options plausible. If the right answer is obvious, people learn nothing, so base distractors on what victims actually believed.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Parent and Senior Citizen Cyber Safety Workshop
prompts.use: Plan a gentle, practical workshop for parents or senior citizens on common frauds.
prompts.prompt: You are a patient community cyber safety educator for families in [CITY / AREA]. Use only the facts I provide below; if something is missing, write [NEEDS INFO] instead of guessing. Audience: [PARENTS / SENIOR CITIZENS / BOTH], approx [N] people. Language: [HINDI / MARATHI / HINGLISH / GUJARATI]. Duration: [MINUTES]. Venue setup: [e.g. society hall, no projector]. Top concerns from the organiser: [LIST]. Plan a workshop covering: OTP and PIN never sharing, fake bank or KYC calls, 'digital arrest' and fake police or CBI calls, pension and life certificate scams, fake customer care numbers from search results, UPI collect requests and QR code scams, WhatsApp account safety (two-step verification), and for parents: children's gaming and social media safety. Include: simple role-play scripts (fictional), a 'pause, check, report' rule, a printable large-font handout with 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in, and how a family member can help. Rules: respectful tone, no tech jargon without explanation, no blaming victims, no step by step fraud methods. Output: agenda, talking points, 2 role-plays, the handout text.
prompts.tip: Ask attendees to save 1930 in their phone contacts during the session itself. It is the single most useful thing they will take home.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Alert Triage Explainer and Walkthrough
prompts.use: Understand and document how to triage a specific SIEM or EDR alert in a lab or authorised environment.
prompts.prompt: You are a patient SOC L2 analyst mentoring an L1 analyst. Use only the facts I provide below; if something is missing, write [NEEDS INFO] instead of guessing. Alert name and source: [e.g. Wazuh rule 5710, Defender alert]. Alert details (redacted): [PASTE FIELDS: timestamp, host, user, process, source and destination IP, rule description]. Environment: [LAB / AUTHORISED EMPLOYER ENVIRONMENT]. Available tools: [LIST]. Explain: 1) What this alert usually means in plain language. 2) Common false positive causes. 3) A triage checklist: what to verify, which logs to pivot to, which questions to ask the user or asset owner. 4) Indicators that would make it a true positive. 5) Severity reasoning. 6) Recommended next actions and when to escalate. 7) A short ticket note template filled from my data. Rules: do not invent log values; if a field is missing, say what to look up. Map to MITRE ATT&CK only where it clearly applies, marked as a suggestion. Defensive guidance only.
prompts.tip: Always write down why you closed an alert as a false positive. That note is what protects you and trains the next analyst.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Phishing Email Analysis of a Sample You Received
prompts.use: Safely analyse a suspicious email you personally received and write a short verdict.
prompts.prompt: You are a SOC analyst specialising in phishing analysis. I received this email myself and want to understand whether it is malicious, without interacting with it. Use only the facts I provide below; if something is missing, write [NEEDS INFO] instead of guessing. Email headers (pasted as text): [HEADERS]. Body text: [BODY]. Links shown, with the actual URLs written defanged like hxxp[:]//example[.]com: [LINKS]. Attachment names and hashes if any (I have not opened them): [DETAILS]. Analyse: sender and reply-to mismatch, SPF / DKIM / DMARC results from the headers, Received chain anomalies, display name tricks, lookalike domains, urgency and social engineering cues, link versus displayed text mismatch, and attachment risk. Output: a verdict (Likely phishing / Suspicious / Likely legitimate) with confidence, an evidence table, IOCs listed in defanged form, safe next steps (report to my email provider or IT team, block sender, check the hash on a reputation service without opening the file, report to cybercrime.gov.in or the impersonated organisation, call 1930 if money or banking credentials were involved), and a 3-line awareness summary I could share with redacted details. Rules: do not visit or reconstruct the phishing page; do not suggest contacting or retaliating against the sender; redact my own email address and personal data.
prompts.tip: Always defang URLs before pasting them anywhere so nobody, including you, can click them by accident.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.

prompts.title: Log Review Summary for a Shift Handover
prompts.use: Summarise a batch of logs or alerts from a lab or authorised environment into a clear handover note.
prompts.prompt: You are a SOC shift lead writing a concise handover. Use only the facts I provide below; if something is missing, write [NEEDS INFO] instead of guessing. Time window: [START TO END, TIMEZONE]. Environment: [LAB / AUTHORISED ENVIRONMENT NAME]. Log or alert extract (redacted): [PASTE]. Tickets worked: [LIST]. Open items: [LIST]. Produce: 1) Shift summary in 3 bullets. 2) Table of notable events (time, source, event, assessment, status). 3) Patterns or anomalies worth watching, with the specific log lines that support each. 4) Open items and recommended owner. 5) Any tuning suggestions for noisy rules. Rules: base every statement on the supplied logs; mark guesses as [HYPOTHESIS]; do not include unredacted personal data, passwords or tokens; keep the whole note under 300 words so the next shift can read it in 2 minutes.
prompts.tip: Lead with what the next shift must act on. Put routine items at the bottom, because a handover is read under time pressure.
prompts.model: Any capable general chat model works. Pick one with a long context window when you paste large inputs.
